key_terms.meaning: The complete Arduino program you upload to the board; stored in flash and restarted on every reset or power-up.
Free editor with a built-in compiler and uploader that sends a sketch to the board over USB.
A plug-in board that stacks on the Arduino headers to add a function such as Wi-Fi, motor drive or a display.
Function that runs once at power-up; used for pinMode() and Serial.begin().
Function that runs again and again forever after setup(); the main body of an Arduino program.
Sets a digital pin as INPUT, OUTPUT or INPUT_PULLUP.
Write HIGH (5 V) or LOW (0 V) to a pin, and read a pin as HIGH or LOW.
On a 10-bit Arduino ADC, one step = Vref ÷ 1024; with Vref = 5 V that is about 4.9 mV.
The 40-pin row on a Raspberry Pi giving 3.3 V digital pins, plus 5 V, 3.3 V and ground pins.
System on Chip; the single chip on a Raspberry Pi holding CPU, GPU and memory controller.
The Debian-based Linux distribution that boots from the microSD card on a Raspberry Pi.
Python library that exposes Raspberry Pi pins as input/output objects; setwarnings, BCM/BOARD numbering.
Higher-level Python library where a pin becomes an object such as LED(17) or Button(2).
Pulse Width Modulation; switching a pin on and off fast so the average voltage, and so LED brightness or motor speed, can be set.
Analog-to-Digital Converter; turns a voltage into a number. Arduino Uno has a 10-bit ADC on pins A0–A5; a Raspberry Pi has none.
Two resistors R1 and R2 giving Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2); used to bring a 5 V signal down to 3.3 V.
A resistor (often 10 kΩ) tying an input pin to supply so a switch reads a clean HIGH when open and LOW when pressed.
Low-cost Wi-Fi microcontroller module with its own GPIO and a small flash; runs its own firmware and connects to a router directly.
Linux single-board computer with a 1 GHz ARM Cortex-A8, 512 MB RAM and two 46-pin headers giving many pins including analog inputs.
Board that combines an ARM application processor running Linux with Arduino-style headers so Arduino shields plug in.
The four repeating steps of a simple IoT node; a safe fallback runs the act step locally when report fails.

takeaways: An Arduino is a microcontroller board: one sketch, no operating system, and pins you drive directly.
Every Arduino sketch is just setup() run once and loop() run forever, so timing depends on how fast loop() finishes.
The Raspberry Pi is a full computer — it boots Linux from a microSD card, which means files, networking and multiple programs, but no guaranteed microsecond timing.
Raspberry Pi GPIO pins are 3.3 V only; a 5 V sensor output must be divided or level-shifted before it touches a pin.
Python on the Pi turns hardware control into short readable code: import a library, create an object, then read or set it.
A sensor converts a physical quantity into a voltage or a digital word; the board converts that into a decision, and the actuator makes the physical change.
A Raspberry Pi cannot read an analog voltage without an external ADC; an Arduino can, on pins A0–A5.
Choose ESP8266 when you need only Wi-Fi and a couple of pins, BeagleBone when you need Linux plus many fast I/O pins, and pcDuino when you need Linux plus Arduino shields.
A simple IoT system is a loop of sense, decide, act and report, and the act step must still work when the network is down.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are judged on board-level detail — pin voltages, resolution, library names, sample code — and on a clear justification of which board suits a stated application.

bank.q: Compare an Arduino board with a Raspberry Pi under four headings: what program runs on it, presence of an operating system, GPIO logic voltage, and typical use in an IoT node.
outline: Arduino: microcontroller, one sketch in flash, setup() then loop(), no OS, 5 V logic on Uno, best for real-time sensing and control.
Raspberry Pi: single-board computer, boots Linux from microSD, runs many processes, 3.3 V GPIO, best for gateway, camera, dashboard, cloud upload.
Arduino handles microsecond timing and analog inputs; Pi does not guarantee timing and has no ADC.
Consequence for design: Pi for compute and connectivity, Arduino for hard real-time or analog work, often used together.

bank.q: Explain the structure of an Arduino sketch. Show the roles of setup() and loop(), and write a sketch that blinks an LED on pin 13 once per second.
outline: setup() runs once after reset; loop() runs forever after that.
pinMode(13, OUTPUT) declares the pin direction in setup().
digitalWrite(13, HIGH); delay(1000); digitalWrite(13, LOW); delay(1000); inside loop().
delay() blocks, so nothing else runs during it; the total loop time sets the blink period.
Comment that variables declared at the top are global and keep their value between loop() passes.

bank.q: List the main hardware features of a Raspberry Pi board and explain what the 40-pin GPIO header provides.
outline: SoC with ARM CPU and GPU, RAM, microSD slot for the OS, USB ports, HDMI, Ethernet or Wi-Fi, power input.
GPIO header: digital input/output pins at 3.3 V, plus 5 V, 3.3 V and ground pins, UART, I2C and SPI pins.
Pins are 3.3 V; 5 V on a signal pin can damage the SoC.
No analog input pins on the header; an external ADC is needed for analog sensors.
Linux boots from microSD, so the same board can run Python scripts, a web server and an MQTT client.

bank.q: Describe the ESP8266 module: its hardware, how it connects to a network, and the two ways it is normally used in an IoT product.
outline: Small Wi-Fi SoC with a few GPIO pins, an ADC pin, flash memory and a serial interface.
Two modes of use: as a Wi-Fi modem driven by an Arduino over AT commands, or as a standalone board programmed directly (NodeMCU style).
Connects to a router as a station, or acts as an access point for configuration.
Low cost and low power make it suitable for sensors and smart switches.
Limitation: few pins and limited memory, so heavy processing belongs on a Pi or a server.

bank.q: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi that reads a push button on GPIO 2 and switches an LED on GPIO 17, using GPIO Zero. Explain each line.
outline: from gpiozero import LED, Button; from signal import pause.
led = LED(17); button = Button(2) creates the two pin objects.
button.when_pressed = led.on; button.when_released = led.off binds events instead of polling.
pause() keeps the program running so the callbacks can fire.
Note Button uses an internal pull-up, so the switch wires between pin and ground; explain active-low logic.
Mention that GPIO.setmode numbering issues disappear because GPIO Zero uses BCM numbers by default.

bank.q: An LM35 temperature sensor is connected to pin A0 of an Arduino Uno with a 5 V reference. Write the code and derive the temperature in degrees Celsius from the ADC value.
outline: LM35 gives 10 mV per degree Celsius, linear, no calibration.
int raw = analogRead(A0) returns 0 to 1023 for 0 to 5 V.
Voltage = raw × 5.0 ÷ 1024; temperature = voltage × 100.
One line version: t = raw * 500.0 / 1024.0.
Print with Serial.println(t); keep loop() slow with delay(1000).
Mention resolution limit: 4.9 mV per step, about 0.49 °C.

bank.q: Explain how an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor is interfaced to an Arduino to measure distance, with the trigger and echo timing and the distance formula.
outline: Four pins: VCC 5 V, GND, Trig input, Echo output.
Send a 10 microsecond HIGH pulse to Trig.
Echo goes HIGH for the round-trip time; measure with pulseIn().
Distance = time × speed of sound ÷ 2 = time × 343 m/s ÷ 2, or time × 0.0343 ÷ 2 in centimetres with time in microseconds.
Add a timeout to pulseIn so a missing echo does not hang the sketch.
Range and accuracy limits, and effect of temperature on the speed of sound.

bank.q: A DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor must be read by a Raspberry Pi. Describe the wiring, the library use, and one problem that arises if the sensor is polled too fast.
outline: DHT11 has one data pin, needs a pull-up of about 10 kΩ to 3.3 V, powered at 3.3 V for a Pi.
Data pin to a chosen GPIO; timing-sensitive one-wire style protocol, so a library is used.
Python: import Adafruit_DHT; humidity, temp = Adafruit_DHT.read_retry(sensor, pin).
DHT11 updates only about once per second or slower; polling faster returns stale or failed reads.
Handle None results and retry; log the values with a timestamp.
The Pi has no ADC, so only digital sensors connect directly; analog sensors need an ADC chip.

bank.q: For each of these three requirements, name the most suitable board and justify it: (a) a battery-run soil moisture node reporting over Wi-Fi, (b) a factory panel needing Linux plus ten fast digital inputs, (c) a lab project reusing an existing Arduino shield but needing a full desktop.
outline: (a) ESP8266: built-in Wi-Fi, low cost, low power, one ADC pin for the moisture probe, deep sleep between readings.
Justify rejection of a Pi: higher power draw, boot time, overkill for one sensor.
(b) BeagleBone Black: Linux plus two 46-pin headers, many pins, and real-time co-processors for fast I/O.
Justify rejection of an Arduino: no OS, no file system, no networking stack without extra hardware.
(c) pcDuino: Linux application processor with Arduino-style headers so the shield plugs in directly.
State the trade-off principle: pins and timing on one side, OS and connectivity on the other.

bank.q: Design a simple IoT system that monitors an overhead water tank, switches the pump off at full level, and alerts the owner on a phone. Cover sensing, decision, action and reporting, and say what happens when the internet link fails.
outline: Sense: level sensor (float switch or ultrasonic) read by the board at a fixed interval.
Decide: a threshold rule — pump off when level is at full, on when below a low mark, with a dead band to stop chattering.
Act: relay or contactor driving the pump; the relay must be rated for motor current.
Report: MQTT publish of level and pump state to a broker; phone app or SMS alert.
Fallback: when the broker is unreachable, the local rule still switches the pump; buffer readings and resend later; a fail-safe timer stops the pump after a maximum run time.
Monitoring: log readings with timestamps, and raise an alert if the level stops changing while the pump runs.

bank.q: A 5 V sensor output is connected directly to a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin. Analyse the fault and evaluate two ways of fixing it, with the resistor values.
outline: The Pi pin is 3.3 V logic; a steady 5 V drives current into the protection diode and can destroy the SoC.
Fix 1: resistive divider, Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2); with R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 2 kΩ, 5 V gives about 3.3 V.
Trade-offs: divider draws continuous current, slows edges, and adds resistor tolerance error.
Fix 2: level shifter or a dedicated logic-level converter; bidirectional, faster, but costs more.
A series resistor alone is not a fix; it limits current but the voltage is still too high.
Check the same issue on Arduino side in reverse: a 3.3 V sensor into a 5 V Arduino usually reads HIGH correctly, but confirm the threshold.

bank.q: Compare two designs for a home automation controller: (a) an ESP8266 node per room with a cloud broker, (b) a Raspberry Pi running a local broker with ESP8266 nodes. Judge them on latency, cost, privacy and behaviour during a network or power failure.
outline: Latency: local broker answers in milliseconds; cloud adds round-trip delay.
Cost: many ESP8266 nodes are cheap; a Pi adds cost but serves many nodes.
Privacy: local broker keeps data in the house; cloud design sends usage patterns to a third party.
Failure: with the cloud design a lost link means no control unless local fallback rules are flashed into the node; a local Pi keeps working over Wi-Fi but dies on a power cut unless on a UPS.
Scalability and maintenance: cloud gives remote access and updates from anywhere; local gives control only inside the home network unless port-forwarding or a VPN is used.
Recommended design: local broker with node-level fallback rules, cloud used only for remote access and long-term storage.

glossary.def: A single chip containing a processor, memory and input/output peripherals, designed to run one fixed program repeatedly.
A complete computer on one printed circuit board with processor, memory, storage slot and input/output ports.
The program stored in a device's non-volatile memory that runs when it powers up.
A small program on the board that accepts a new sketch over USB and starts the stored program.
To translate source code into machine instructions for the target board before it can run.
General-Purpose Input/Output; a digital pin whose direction and level the program controls.
The voltage that represents digital 1 on a pin; 5 V on most Arduino boards and 3.3 V on a Raspberry Pi.
A reusable plastic board with connected holes for building circuits without soldering.
An electrically operated switch that lets a low-voltage board control a high-voltage or high-current load.
A transistor, often with a base resistor and a flyback diode, used between a board pin and a load that needs more current.
A sensor whose output is a continuously varying voltage proportional to the measured quantity.
A sensor that outputs a discrete value, either one bit or a coded word over a bus such as I2C.
A two-wire bus (clock and data) that lets one board talk to many addressed sensor chips.
A four-wire synchronous serial bus used for fast links to displays, memory and some sensors.
A device that converts an electrical command into physical action, such as a motor, relay, solenoid or buzzer.
Ignoring the brief contact chatter of a mechanical switch, in hardware with a capacitor or in software with a short delay.
A low-power mode where a module shuts most circuits off and wakes on a timer or event, used to extend battery life.
A lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol where devices send topics to a broker and subscribers receive them.
The server in a publish-subscribe system that receives messages on topics and forwards them to subscribers.
Doing part of the decision on the local device instead of sending all raw data to the cloud.
A design in which a loss of power, signal or network leaves the system in a safe state, such as the pump switching off.
One device in an IoT system that senses, acts and communicates with the rest of the system.
